title: The Saints Will Judge the World
english: Paul says: Do you wish me to bring a wise rebuke upon those who have sinned, as with a rod? Or shall I deal with you in a spirit of gentleness, as in love, and pass the matter by in silence (1 Corinthians 4:21)? But rebuke was better for them, for it would cut off at once the dreadful sin, the slackness, and the very attempt at such lawlessness. Of this the inspired Scripture also spoke concerning the people of Israel, through the voice of Joel: “A son and his father went in to the same girl, so as to profane the name of their God” (Amos 2:7).

He says that such fornication is not heard of even among the Gentiles (1 Corinthians 5:1). For he had heard somewhere, we may suppose, of Theseus, who was roused to fury against his own son, cursed him, and even killed him, after the stepmother had set him against the boy; and of certain others whom the poets in their fine verse mocked on similar charges.

“To deliver such a man to Satan for the destruction of the flesh” (1 Corinthians 5:5). By handing over the fornicator to the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved, Paul showed what is meant by “The kingdom of heaven is not in word but in power” (1 Corinthians 4:20). For this is a clear sign of the marvelous authority given to him from above. For our Lord Jesus Christ has honored the saints.

“To go to law before the unrighteous, and not before the saints?” (1 Corinthians 6:1). He calls saints those who have been sanctified in the Spirit, and unrighteous those who have not yet believed, since they are all too ready to go after any evil whatever. For those who do not yet know him who is God by nature and in truth leave no outrage untried.

“Do you not know that the saints will judge the world?” (1 Corinthians 6:2). They will judge it, not by sitting in every case as judges on the bench, for “there is one Lawgiver and Judge” (James 4:12), but by the dignity of their life and their readiness to obey in everything. By this they all but pass sentence on the sin of the world, because the people of the world did not become their imitators. For we are all of one nature: we have all been given the earth for a mother and live in these perishable bodies. But if some of us have become lovers of God and good, what plea will be left to help, before the divine judgment seat, those who chose an inglorious and accursed life? For though they could have been honored equally with the others, they went of their own will after every kind of outrage.

“Do you not know that we shall judge angels? How much more the things of this life!” (1 Corinthians 6:3). We shall read the verse as a question, with a pause; this is to be read as a question, with a pause: For who would dare to say that you are unworthy of such petty courts (1 Corinthians 6:2), you who judge the world by the brightness of your life? Then he adds a reason for what he has said, and confirms the force of his argument by setting the greater case beside it. By angels here he does not mean the holy angels, but rather the apostates, who did not keep their own first rank (Jude 6). Though they were from above and not weighed down with bodies made from earth, they will be condemned by the saints in the same way as the world, through the goodness of the saints, and stand accused of every kind of shameful deed. If, then, the saints are better than angels, how could they be unworthy of the smallest courts, those that deal with worldly affairs?

“If, then, you have courts for matters of this life” (1 Corinthians 6:4). To judge the matters of this life is a very small thing, worth nothing to those in the church who are truly upright. We have been taught this, too, by the Lord. For someone came to him and said, “Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.” But he said to him, “Man, who made me a judge or divider over you?” (Luke 12:13–14). It would better suit the wiser members of the church to judge spiritual things, and to test with skill the teaching about the faith. This is counted among the good gifts given from above and through the Spirit; for to some is given a word of wisdom and a word of knowledge, and to others the discerning of spirits (1 Corinthians 12:8–10).
“Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ?” (1 Corinthians 6:15). How could our bodies be members of Christ? We have him within ourselves both in a way the senses perceive…
translator_notes: Copy-text: PG 74, Fragmenta in 1 Cor (Greek). Original English from the Greek; no English base used.

The Greek of this section opens with 'ἐν ἀγάπῃ;', the last words of the lemma 1 Corinthians 4:21; the whole lemma is translated at the end of the previous section, so this section begins with Cyril's comment. 'Paul says:' renders φησίν.

The section ends mid-sentence: 'ἔχομεν αὐτὸν ἐν ἑαυτοῖς αἰσθητῶς' continues 'τε καὶ νοητῶς' at the head of the next section. The English ends with an ellipsis at the break, and the next section completes the sentence ('…and in a spiritual way'). αἰσθητῶς = perceptibly, by the senses (Cyril goes on to speak of sharing Christ's holy flesh).

Cyril attributes the quotation to Joel ('διὰ φωνῆς Ἰωήλ'), but the words are Amos 2:7 (LXX: 'καὶ υἱὸς καὶ ὁ πατὴρ αὐτοῦ εἰσεπορεύοντο πρὸς τὴν αὐτὴν παιδίσκην, ὅπως βεβηλώσωσι τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ θεοῦ αὐτῶν'). The English keeps Cyril's 'Joel' and cites the true locus.

Theseus: the myth of Hippolytus, whom his father Theseus cursed and destroyed after the stepmother Phaedra accused him falsely. 'διαβεβλημένον ἐκ μητρυιᾶς' is taken with Theseus (the stepmother 'had set him against the boy'); it could also be read of the son ('slandered by his stepmother'). The sense of the story is the same either way.
'ἡγιασμένους ἐν πνεύματι' rendered 'sanctified in the Spirit' (Holy Spirit), as Cyril uses the phrase; the printed text has lowercase πνεύματι.
'Εἷς γὰρ ὁ νομοθέτης καὶ κριτής' is James 4:12; Lawgiver and Judge capitalised since they name God.
'μονονουχὶ καθορίζοντες τοῦ κόσμου τὴν ἁμαρτίαν' rendered 'all but pass sentence on the sin of the world'.

'Ἀναγνωσόμεθα δὲ τὸν στίχον ὡς ἐν ἐρωτήσει καὶ ὑποστιγμῇ, ὡς κατὰ ἐρώτησιν ἀναγνωστέον τοῦτο καθ' ὑποστιγμήν' is repetitive in the Greek (perhaps a doublet); both clauses are kept. ὑποστιγμή is a minor stop (a pause like a comma). The question that follows paraphrases 1 Corinthians 6:2 ('unworthy of such petty courts'), cited inline.
'τοὺς τὴν ἑαυτῶν ἀρχὴν οὐ τετηρηκότας' is Jude 6 ('who did not keep their own first rank'); cited inline.
ἐπιείκεια / ἐπιεικής rendered 'goodness' / 'truly upright' in this passage, where it means moral excellence rather than mildness.
Luke 12:13–14 is quoted nearly word for word.
'λόγος σοφίας ... λόγος γνώσεως ... διάκρισις πνευμάτων' gathers 1 Corinthians 12:8 and 12:10; cited as 12:8–10.
baehrens: PG 74; Fragmenta in 1 Cor u02 rem early

title: Members of Christ and Sin Against the Body
english: …and in a spiritual way. For he dwells in our hearts through the Spirit (compare Ephesians 3:17), and we have also shared in his holy flesh; so we have been made holy in two ways. He has come to dwell in us as life and as the giver of life, so that through himself he might abolish the death that had fallen upon our members. This frees us from corruption and from the snares of death, and raises us above the passions of the flesh. We also receive within ourselves the unleavened teaching of the divine oracles (compare 1 Corinthians 5:8), which nourishes the ruling part of the soul, and we live together with Christ, spiritually of course, having overcome the passions of the flesh.

If, then, he is “the head of the body, the church” (Colossians 1:18), we are its members, each one in particular. So whenever we fall into unseemly pleasures, then, precisely then, we will sin against him whose members we have become. For we will be, as it were, handing over what is his to fornicators: his members are defiled by sin and are made members of a prostitute (1 Corinthians 6:15). For just as the man who is joined to a woman will be one body with her, so also the one who is bound to God spiritually will be one spirit with him (1 Corinthians 6:16–17). For we have become “partakers of the divine nature” (2 Peter 1:4), and we have been joined to him and made holy through the Spirit in Christ.
From the third book on the Letter to the Corinthians, by the same Cyril.
“Every sin that a person commits is outside the body, but the one who commits fornication sins against his own body” (1 Corinthians 6:18).

Someone might say: “Tell me, how will the murderer carry out his murder? Is it not by bloodshed? And if someone chooses to find fault with others, is it not with his tongue that he is such a man? What offense, then, could be committed other than through the body? Will the bearer of the Spirit, then, turn out after all to have spoken falsely?” By no means! For he speaks in Christ (compare 2 Corinthians 2:17), and Christ is the truth (John 14:6); so he will be truthful.

Suppose we look into the matter this way: if someone happens to choose to be perverse in his ways, he will surely be so toward others and not toward himself. The murderer will kill not himself but others; the reviler will insult not himself but others; the greedy man will wrong not himself but others; and in each outrageous deed that is done you will find the same course. In this sense, then, “every sin is outside the body, but the one who commits fornication sins against his own body.” For he will be caught wronging his very own body, and I will say in what way.

The members of our body, if through purity they have remained members of Christ, will surely share in the life and glory that come from him; for “he will transform the body of our lowliness to be conformed to the body of his glory” (Philippians 3:21). But if they should become members of a prostitute, how could they receive that transformation and the spiritual splendor of being conformed to him? For when earthly bodies have been raised at the time of the resurrection, “the righteous will shine like the sun” (Matthew 13:43). The ungodly, the profane, and those who have lived outrageously will indeed be raised, yet they will not go on to live the glorious life; they remain without any share in glory. For they will rise not “in judgment, nor in the council of the righteous” (Psalm 1:5), but for penalty and punishment, for they will go down into the outer darkness (compare Matthew 25:30). For how can what is being punished be in glory? And he adds something more, which has no small power to persuade us to hate the accursed pleasure of the body.

The one who murders, the one who dishonors, and the one who reviles commit the sin with the body, yet they do it against others. In this sense it is said, “Every sin is outside the body,” but the one who commits fornication wrongs his very own body. Through purity our bodies remain members of Christ and share in the life and glory that come from him; but if the body is defiled, it is deprived of that glory.
“Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you?” (1 Corinthians 6:19). For “the Spirit of adoption” (Romans 8:15) has come to dwell in us…
translator_notes: The section opens mid-sentence: the previous section ends ἔχομεν αὐτὸν ἐν ἑαυτοῖς αἰσθητῶς and this one continues τε καὶ νοητῶς ('we have him in ourselves both perceptibly and spiritually'). The break is marked with a leading ellipsis.

αἰσθητῶς τε καὶ νοητῶς is then explained in reverse order: νοητῶς = the indwelling through the Spirit, αἰσθητῶς = sharing in Christ's holy flesh (the Eucharist). 'Made holy in two ways' renders ἡγιάσμεθά τε διττῶς.
Column numbers 264 and 266 and the transcription's page numbers 6 and 7 are omitted. The stray full stop in εἰ τῇδέ πη. τὸ χρῆμα is a slip in the transcription and is ignored.

τῶν τοῦ θανάτου βρόχων 'the snares of death' may echo Psalm 18:5 (LXX 17:6, παγίδες θανάτου) but the wording differs; left as a possible echo, not cited inline. συζῶμεν Χριστῷ may echo Romans 6:8; not cited.
ἀμείνους ποιεῖ παθῶν σαρκικῶν: 'raises us above the passions of the flesh' (literally 'makes us better than'); the sense is superiority over the passions.
πόρνοις γὰρ ὥσπερ τὰ αὐτοῦ χαριούμεθα: the source has masculine πόρνοις, rendered 'fornicators'; χαριούμεθα (future of χαρίζομαι) is 'we will be handing over', as a gift. 'As it were' keeps ὥσπερ.
ἔσται in the 6:16–17 paraphrase is future ('will be one body … will be one spirit'); kept, as Cyril changes Paul's ἐστιν.
ΤΟΥ ΑΥΤΟΥ ΚΥΡΙΛΛΟΥ ΕΚ ΤΟΥ Γ ΤΟΜΟΥ ΤΗΣ ΠΡΟΣ ΚΟΡΙΝΘΙΟΥΣ is the catena heading for a new fragment; kept as its own short line. τόμος rendered 'book'.

The objection 'Tell me, how will the murderer …' is placed in the mouth of the imagined objector (φαίη τις ἄν) down to 'spoken falsely?'; μὴ γένοιτο begins Cyril's answer. ὁ πνευματοφόρος is Paul, whose claim in 6:18 the objector seems to contradict.
δι' αἵματος (literally 'through blood') is rendered 'by bloodshed'; the objector means the murderer acts by bodily violence.
σκαιὸς … τοὺς τρόπους 'perverse in his ways'. ἐφ' ἑκάστῳ τῶν ἐκτόπων τινὰ τῶν δρωμένων τοιαύτην εὑρήσεις ὁδόν: 'in each outrageous deed that is done you will find the same course'.

ἐγερθήσονται μὲν, οὐ μὴν ἔτι … διαβιώσονται: the wicked are raised but do not live the glorious life. The resurrection is of all; the glory is for the pure alone. μένουσι is present in the source ('they remain') and kept.
κατοιχήσονται 'they will go down' (the verb of departing to the underworld).
προσεπάγει δέ τι καὶ ἕτερον: Paul 'adds something more', namely 6:19–20, which follows. οὐκ ἀνικάνως ἔχον 'which has no small power' renders the litotes.
The paragraph beginning Ἐπειδὴ καὶ ὁ φονεύων is a second, shorter catena fragment on the same verse; it is translated in full even though it repeats the argument.
The section ends mid-sentence at τὸ τῆς υἱοθεσίας Πνεῦμα; the continuation (τουτέστι τὸ Ἅγιον, ἐν ᾧ κράζομεν …) opens the next section. A trailing ellipsis marks the break.
baehrens: PG 74; Fragmenta in 1 Cor u02 rem mid

title: Temples of God, and Paul’s Counsel to the Unmarried
english: …that is, the Holy Spirit, “by whom we cry, Abba, Father” (Romans 8:15). And we have been bought at a price (1 Corinthians 6:20), since Christ, the Savior of us all, laid down his own life for us (compare 1 John 3:16). We are, then, temples of the living God (2 Corinthians 6:16); for Christ makes his dwelling in us through the Holy Spirit, and in his own nature he has also the Father and God, from whom he came forth in essence. For he himself said, “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him” (John 14:23).

So let foul-smelling pleasure be far from our minds, as from a temple of God, and let the sweet fragrance of self-control rise up instead, like incense. Let us present “our bodies as a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God, our reasonable worship” (Romans 12:1). For we were bought “not with perishable things, with silver or gold, but with precious blood” (1 Peter 1:18–19), as it is written. Let us therefore serve him who bought us; let us present ourselves to him for obedience (Romans 6:16), “and our members as instruments of righteousness to God” (Romans 6:13). For it is written, “The body is not for fornication but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body” (1 Corinthians 6:13). So when we keep the members of the body free of the defilement that comes from love of the flesh, then the Lord too will be for the body; for he dwells among the holy, being holy by nature, as God.
“To the unmarried and the widows I say: it is good for them if they remain as I am” (1 Corinthians 7:8).

The people of Israel were found to be very fickle and easily carried away toward anything at all that pleased them. For this very reason they were rightly barred by the law from giving rulings of their own. For of the commandments it says, “To them nothing may be added, and from them nothing may be taken away” (Ecclesiastes 3:14; compare Deuteronomy 4:2). But those who brought in the decrees of the Gospel had minds set firmly on the good and had Christ himself speaking within them (compare 2 Corinthians 13:3). So they rightly took courage to give their words of guidance with great authority, even where some matter of conduct was not laid down in the sacred writings.

The inspired Paul was such a man. “I say,” he writes, “to the unmarried and the widows, it is good for them if they remain as I am,” and so on (1 Corinthians 7:8). Where we have no divine law, he has of necessity put “I say”; but where Christ was the one giving the command, he says “I command,” adding at once, “not I, but the Lord” (1 Corinthians 7:10). Yet what necessary thing did Christ overlook when he gave the law? Do those who lead us into the mysteries devise something better? And how could it be anything but ignorant and utterly senseless to think that what comes from Christ is not complete? What, then, shall we say?

The divine preaching of the Gospel did not forbid marriage, since God, I think, measures the commandment to human nature. For when the Pharisees, testing him, asked the Lord “whether it is lawful to put away his wife” (Matthew 19:3) for a cause other than fornication, he told them that whoever puts away “his wife, except on the ground of fornication, causes her to commit adultery” (Matthew 5:32; compare Matthew 19:9). At this the disciples said to him, “If this is how the case stands between a man and his wife, it is better not to marry.” And he said to them, “There are eunuchs who were born so from their mother’s womb, and there are eunuchs who were made eunuchs by men, and there are eunuchs who made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. Let the one who is able to accept this accept it” (Matthew 19:10, 12). For he set it before those who wish to achieve it, but he did not bring it under law, since he knew that not all are able to master the impulses of the flesh.

In this the shadow of the law (compare Hebrews 10:1) also has something entirely like it. It commanded that the various kinds of sacrifice be offered to the glory of God: some for sin and for sins of ignorance, others for cleansing and the casting away of filth, and also those on the Sabbath, those at the new moon, and those at the feasts. But besides these it also allowed…
translator_notes: The section opens mid-sentence, continuing the Romans 8:15 quotation from the previous section; marked with a leading ellipsis.
Column numbers 267, 268 and 269 and the transcription's page number 8 are omitted.
ἔχων ἐν ἰδίᾳ φύσει καὶ τὸν ἐξ οὗ πέφηνεν οὐσιωδῶς Πατέρα καὶ Θεόν: Christ has the Father in his own nature, and has come forth from him in essence (οὐσιωδῶς).

ἀπέστω … ἡ κάκοσμος ἡδονή and ἀναφοιτάτω … ἡ εὐοσμία are third-person imperatives, rendered 'let … be far' and 'let … rise up'. ἐν τάξει θυμιαμάτων 'like incense' (literally 'in the order of incense offerings').
τὴν λογικὴν λατρείαν 'our reasonable worship': λογικός here means worship fitting a rational being, in contrast to animal sacrifice.
ὅπλα δικαιοσύνης 'instruments of righteousness'; ὅπλον can also mean 'weapon'.
κατοικεῖ γὰρ ἐν ἁγίοις ἅγιος ὢν κατὰ φύσιν ὡς Θεός: 'he dwells among the holy, being holy by nature, as God'. A possible echo of LXX Isaiah 57:15 (ἐν ἁγίοις ἀναπαυόμενος) is not cited inline.
εὐπάροιστοι: 'easily carried away' (from παροιστράω, to be driven wild); κατεφωρῶντο 'were found'; λίαν is taken with the adjectives ('very fickle').

τὸ χρῆναι γνωμοδοτεῖν παρῄρηντο νόμῳ: Israel was barred by law from giving rulings of their own, i.e. from adding opinions to the commandments; this is Cyril's contrast with the apostles, who may give counsel beyond what is written.

οἱ … εἰσηγηταί 'those who brought in' the Gospel decrees are the apostles. οἱ μυσταγωγοί in the rhetorical question ('those who lead us into the mysteries') means the same apostles as teachers of the mysteries.

The three questions 'what necessary thing did Christ overlook … something better … not complete?' are Cyril's own rhetorical questions raising the difficulty; τί οὖν ἐροῦμεν introduces his answer that the Gospel did not forbid marriage. Christ omitted nothing necessary; virginity is counsel, not law.
ἐπιμετροῦντος … τοῦ Θεοῦ τῇ ἀνθρώπου φύσει τὴν ἐντολήν: 'God … measures the commandment to human nature', i.e. fits it to what human nature can bear.
μὴ ἐπὶ πορνείᾳ stands between the Pharisees' question and ὅτι; it is attached to the question ('for a cause other than fornication'), which fits Matthew 19:9.
προὔθηκε … οὐ μὴν ὑπήγαγε νόμῳ: 'he set it before … but he did not bring it under law'. κατευμεγεθεῖν 'master'.
The sacrifices on Sabbath, new moon and feasts summarise the calendar of Numbers 28–29; no single verse is quoted, so it is not cited inline.

The section ends mid-sentence at ἠφίει γεμὴν πρὸς τούτοις καὶ; the object (ἑκουσιάζεσθαί τινας) opens the next section. A trailing ellipsis marks the break; the subject of ἠφίει is taken to be the law, as with προστέταχε.
baehrens: PG 74; Fragmenta in 1 Cor u02 rem close
